label: Candid
rationale: Straight Ahead is Abbey Lincoln's Candid debut and the record that turned her from a standards singer into a writer-performer of her own material -- the moment the Penguin Guide singles out, writing of 'Retribution' that 'for the first time, Lincoln seems willing to confront her music rather than stand up-stage of it' [S1] (obs). Consensus across independent listing traditions is strong for a vocal record: AllMusic rates it five stars and Scott Yanow calls it 'one of Abbey Lincoln's greatest recordings'; MusicHound Jazz gives five, the Virgin Encyclopedia of Jazz four, the Penguin Guide three and a half, and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide three [S1] (obs). Session gravity: this is a Max Roach-circle date -- Lincoln's partner on drums, with Booker Little, Julian Priester, Eric Dolphy, Coleman Hawkins, Walter Benton, Mal Waldron and Art Davis, the same Candid/Nola Penthouse circle that made We Insist! Max Roach's Freedom Now Suite a few months earlier [S1,S2,S3] (obs). Lineage: it sits directly downstream of the canon's We Insist! (1960) -- same label, same room, same supervisor, the same Booker Little / Julian Priester / Walter Benton / Coleman Hawkins front line and the same singer -- and it is the record on which Lincoln begins setting her own texts, the line that runs to People in Me (1973) [S1,S2,S3] (inf). It still plays: 'Retribution', 'In the Red', 'When Malindy Sings' and the Langston Hughes / Randy Weston 'African Lady' are the discovery side of the album, and the reading of 'Left Alone' is one of the great Billie Holiday tributes [S1,S3] (obs). Gap: Lincoln is the canon's most conspicuous absence as a leader -- she appears in the database only as a singer on We Insist!, and no Lincoln-led album is present in any status (verified against _jazzcanon.album, 2026-10-11) (obs).

personnel_record.notes: One session: Nola Penthouse Sound Studios, New York City, February 22, 1961 (S2, S3, S7). Producer/supervisor Nat Hentoff; engineer Bob d'Orleans (S4, S7 — the engineer is not named in the Wikipedia or jazzdisco entries). Original issue Candid CJM 8015 (mono) / CJS 9015 (stereo), 45-602 issued 'Straight Ahead'/'Retribution'; Barnaby KZ 31037 in 1972, Candid CCD 79015 in 1988, 2022 Candid 180g remaster 30151 (S2, S3, S4). Side layout: the original LP credit block (S7) places arrangement credits at positions A1-A3 and B1-B4, and jazzdiscography's issue index lists a-01 to a-03 and b-01 to b-03 for the first six titles (S3), so side A is tracks 1-3 and side B is tracks 4-7; the recorded track order follows Wikipedia and jazzdisco (S1, S2). Two source conflicts are preserved rather than resolved: (1) conga coverage — 'African Lady' only per S2 and S7, tracks 6 and 7 per S3, recorded as epistemic unk on both conga players; (2) the fourth title is printed as 'Blue Monk' by Wikipedia and jazzdisco but appears on the original LP issue index as 'Monkery's The Blues', the lyric version of 'Blue Monk' (S3) — Wikipedia credits Abbey Lincoln alongside Thelonious Monk as composer, jazzdiscography credits Monk alone, and both are recorded. Timings differ slightly between sources: Wikipedia gives 5:24/4:05/8:32/6:39/6:48/3:46/3:50, jazzdiscography's LP index gives 5:18/4:00/8:23/6:32/6:42/3:42 (S1, S3); Wikipedia's are recorded. Per-track personnel is not documented for this single-session date beyond the conga restriction — the sources present one ensemble for the session — so each track's personnel array carries the full session ensemble and is marked epistemic inf rather than obs, and track_assignments_complete is false. Eric Dolphy's piccolo and the arrangement credits are recorded in the personnel notes because the taxonomy has no entry for them.

ballot.case_for: The strongest case is that this is Lincoln’s defining transition into a writer-performer: the Penguin assessment quoted in S1 says that on “Retribution” she first seems willing to confront her music directly. Its Candid/Nola Penthouse session brings together Max Roach, Booker Little, Eric Dolphy, Coleman Hawkins, Julian Priester, and Mal Waldron, linking it closely to the canon’s We Insist! (S1–S3). Multiple guidebooks rate it highly, and tracks including “Retribution,” “African Lady,” and “Left Alone” make a compelling discovery case for Lincoln as a leader.
ballot.case_against: The critical record is positive but not unqualified: Penguin gives it 3.5 stars and Rolling Stone 3, while the dossier’s review quotations are reported through Wikipedia rather than directly sourced (S1). The album’s tightly arranged vocal focus may offer less extended instrumental exploration than a listener seeking an instrumental post-bop showcase expects. Its personnel and lineage make it a powerful view of the Roach-Candid circle, but the case that it initiated a forward-moving post-bop lineage is less established than its value as a defining Lincoln statement.
ballot.disagreement: Gemini rates the album consensus_core, emphasizing Lincoln’s definitive artistic transformation and the ensemble’s historical importance; MiniMax rates it contested, judging the critical ceiling, vocal-led format, and more summative than forward-looking character to be substantial counterweights. The shared assessment supports strong priority, but the tier disagreement should remain visible.
ballot.recommendation: John should weigh this as a strong, contested candidate: its defining importance for Lincoln and exceptional session connections argue for it, while its qualified critical standing and vocal-centered format keep it short of consensus_core.
